item.passage:
Joel Mercer's tent went over the hedge on a Thursday and came back on Sunday with a yellow patch in its floor.

Hana and Joel had been passing things across that hedge since they were six: comic books, a flashlight with a cracked lens, once a box turtle that had wandered into Hana's yard and needed, Joel said, a second opinion. The tent was the largest thing either of them had ever handed over. It was a green two-person dome, and Joel had paid for half of it with two summers of mowing the Ostranders' lawn. When he lent it to Hana for her class camping trip to Cutter's Lake, he gave one instruction. "Clear the ground first," he said. "Every stick."

She cleared most of them. On the second morning she found a hole the size of a coin near the door, right where she had been sleeping, and under it the stub of a root she had taken for a lump of dirt in the dark.

On Saturday night she cut a square from an old rain jacket, borrowed her mother's sewing kit, and stitched the square over the hole, sealing the edges with glue. The stitches were small and even. The patch was also impossible to miss, bright yellow against the green.

She thought about rolling the tent with the floor tucked inside. Joel might go months before he unrolled it, and by then it would be an old story. Instead she rolled it with the patch on the outside, where it would be the first thing he saw.

On Sunday she could have passed it back over the hedge. Instead she carried it around by the sidewalk and stood on the Mercers' porch for a long minute before she rang the bell. When Joel opened the door, she unrolled the tent across the boards, told him about the root, and said that if the patch failed she would pay for a new floor.

Joel crouched and ran his thumb around the edge of the yellow square. Then he folded back a corner of the floor at the far end and showed her a second patch, gray and smaller, sewn in loose, uneven loops.

"Scout camp, the first week I had it," he said. "I never told my dad." He looked at the two patches side by side. "Yours is better."

"I cleared most of them," Hana said.

"Next time clear every stick."

"Next time?"

He was already rolling the tent up, patch and all. "That's what I said."

That evening something came over the hedge and landed on Hana's back step: a roll of waterproof seam tape with a strip of masking tape stuck to it. On the strip, in Joel's square capitals, were three words: FOR NEXT TIME.

On the inside of the pantry door,
behind the brooms, where guests never look,
my family is written in pencil:
short dashes climbing toward the hinge,

each one a name and a date
in whoever's hand was nearest.
My mother's print is square and quick.
My father's leans as if into wind.

The lowest line is my brother's,
age two, the spring he would stand
only if someone held a cracker
just above his head.

Mine begin at three and climb
in steps as uneven as a stair
built by guesswork: a long jump
the summer I turned eleven,

then almost nothing for a year,
then two lines close as twins
where I measured twice to be sure
and came out the same both times.

Someone measured the dog once,
up on her back legs for a crust,
and wrote BISCUIT, 4 FT,
which everyone agrees was cheating.

Last spring my parents painted the kitchen
a color called Oat. They painted the walls,
the cupboards, the ceiling, every inch of trim,
and stopped at the pantry door.

My father taped along its edges
the way you would tape a window
before a storm, and left it
the old yellow, smudged and scuffed.

I have been the same height two years now.
Still, when I reach for the flour,
I stand with my back against the door,
lay my hand flat on my head,

and slide it back to the wood
the way I was taught, and look,
and find myself where I was last time.
Nobody writes it down. It is enough

to stand there in the narrow light
with all of them beside me on the door,
the hands that held the pencil,
the hand that held the cracker,

the dog still reaching for her crust.

When I was eleven, my father offered me twenty-five cents for every shirt I ironed, and I accepted the job as though he had offered me a seat in government.

He drove a delivery truck for a bakery and wore a white shirt every day, with his name stitched in blue thread above the pocket. For years he had ironed them himself on Sunday nights, five in a row, with the radio on. He did it fast and not especially well. I had watched him for years, and I believed I could improve on his method.

I began with research. From the library I borrowed a book on household management, published long before I was born, that devoted four pages to the shirt. It gave an order: collar first, then cuffs, then sleeves, then the back, then the two fronts. I copied the order onto an index card and taped it to the end of the ironing board. I tested the iron on a dish towel before every session, and I kept the spray bottle filled with water that had stood overnight, because the book said so.

My first shirt took forty minutes. My father, who could do one in about six, came in twice to see whether his daughter had fallen asleep. When I finished, I hung it on the back of the kitchen door and asked him to inspect it. He looked at the front and the back and said it would do. I asked him what "do" meant, and whether there were levels above it.

By November I was down to twelve minutes a shirt, and I had begun to keep records in a spiral notebook: the date, the time taken, and a remark. Most of the remarks were about cuffs.

Then, one evening in December, I left the iron face down on a shirt front while I answered the telephone, and when I came back there was a brown triangle across the pocket, right through his name. I stood in the kitchen holding the shirt and calculated that, at twenty-five cents a shirt, I would be working about two months to pay for it. My father looked at the scorch and said he had a sweater that would cover it. He wore that shirt under the sweater all winter, and I never heard him mention it. In my notebook, under that date, the remark reads only: Phone.

I ironed his shirts until I left for college, and in time I could do one in five minutes, faster than he ever had. I have rarely prepared for anything as thoroughly as I prepared for those shirts. I think now that the shirts were the occasion, and something else was the point. He had handed me a thing he wore every day, with his name on it, and even at eleven I understood that this was a serious thing to be handed.

Every spring, wildlife rehabilitation centers fill with birds that never needed rescuing. They arrive in shoeboxes and margarine tubs, carried in by people who found them on a lawn or a sidewalk: small, fluffy, stubby-tailed birds that hop instead of fly and look, to any reasonable person, abandoned.

Most of them are fledglings, and most of them were fine. For many songbirds, leaving the nest is a stage, not a graduation. The young leave once their feathers are mostly grown but before they can fly well, and for several days they live on the ground or in low branches, practicing short flights while their parents go on feeding them. A parent may stay away for many minutes between visits, and it often keeps out of sight while a person stands nearby. The finder sees a lone chick and concludes that it is an orphan. In many cases the parents are in the next tree, waiting for the finder to leave.

A doe commonly leaves her fawn lying alone in the grass for hours at a stretch, returning to nurse it, because a fawn with little scent of its own is safer hidden by itself than standing beside its large and easily noticed mother. Picking up a healthy fledgling is an act of kindness that costs the bird the best care it could have had.

The better habit is harder, because it means doing less. Watch from a distance for an hour. Keep cats indoors. If the bird is featherless or plainly injured, call a rehabilitator, many of whom will talk a finder through what to do. And let go of the old story that a parent will abandon a chick that smells of human hands; most songbirds will do no such thing.

In 1899 the houses of Oriel had names, owners, and reputations, but they had no numbers. A letter for the Tolliver family might be marked "Tolliver, brick house past the tannery," and the postmaster, who had known the Tollivers for thirty years, would hold it at the counter until one of them came in. Most people collected their mail once or twice a week. The system was slow, but it was friendly, and in a town of eighteen hundred people it worked.

That spring the postal service offered Oriel free delivery to every door, on one condition: each house had to carry a number, and each street a sign. The town council voted to accept and handed the job to its clerk, a former surveyor named Miriam Holt.

Residents doubted the whole idea. Everyone already knew where everyone lived, they said, and the postmaster knew it best of all. One letter to the Oriel Courier asked why a man who had lived on Cannery Road for forty years should now be known by a figure, "like a coat at the theater." Another writer predicted that the numbers would soon be used to raise taxes. A few people simply refused to nail them up.

Holt began by walking every street with a surveyor's chain. Instead of numbering houses one after another, she numbered them by distance, assigning one number to every twenty feet of frontage, with odd numbers on one side of the street and even on the other. On Cannery Road, where the houses stood far apart, the numbers jumped from 4 to 30 to 58. People laughed at the gaps. Holt answered that she was leaving room.

Delivery began in January 1900. Within a year the postmaster reported that the line at his counter had all but disappeared and that two carriers could cover the town in a morning. The first real test came in 1904, when a fire broke out at night in a house set back from Cannery Road. The man who ran to the firehouse was a peddler passing through, who could not have named the family, but he had read the number on the gatepost. The fire company drove past three dark houses straight to 58.

Over the next twenty years Oriel doubled in size. Eleven new houses went up on Cannery Road alone, in the gaps that had been laughed at, and each of them took a number Holt had set aside, so that the old houses kept their numbers. Asked late in life whether she had expected the town to grow so much, Holt said that she had only measured the land. Land, she said, was patient. It would wait for its houses.

In 1899 the houses of Oriel had names, owners, and reputations, but they had no numbers. A letter for the Tolliver family might be marked "Tolliver, brick house past the tannery," and the postmaster, who had known the Tollivers for thirty years, would hold it at the counter until one of them came in. Most people collected their mail once or twice a week. The system was slow, but it was friendly, and in a town of eighteen hundred people it worked.

That spring the postal service offered Oriel free delivery to every door, on one condition: each house had to carry a number, and each street a sign. The town council voted to accept and handed the job to its clerk, a former surveyor named Miriam Holt.

Residents doubted the whole idea. Everyone already knew where everyone lived, they said, and the postmaster knew it best of all. One letter to the Oriel Courier asked why a man who had lived on Cannery Road for forty years should now be known by a figure, "like a coat at the theater." Another writer predicted that the numbers would soon be used to raise taxes. A few people simply refused to nail them up.

Holt began by walking every street with a surveyor's chain. Instead of numbering houses one after another, she numbered them by distance, assigning one number to every twenty feet of frontage, with odd numbers on one side of the street and even on the other. On Cannery Road, where the houses stood far apart, the numbers jumped from 4 to 30 to 58. People laughed at the gaps. Holt answered that she was leaving room.

Delivery began in January 1900. Within a year the postmaster reported that the line at his counter had all but disappeared and that two carriers could cover the town in a morning. The first real test came in 1904, when a fire broke out at night in a house set back from Cannery Road. The man who ran to the firehouse was a peddler passing through, who could not have named the family, but he had read the number on the gatepost. The fire company drove past three dark houses straight to 58.

Over the next twenty years Oriel doubled in size. Eleven new houses went up on Cannery Road alone, in the gaps that had been laughed at, and each of them took a number Holt had set aside, so that the old houses kept their numbers. Asked late in life whether she had expected the town to grow so much, Holt said that she had only measured the land. Land, she said, was patient. It would wait for its houses.

Draw a small cross on a card, and about three inches to its right a dot the size of a pencil eraser. Close your left eye, stare at the cross with your right, and slowly bring the card toward your face. At a distance of roughly a foot, the dot will vanish. Keep looking at the cross and move the card a little nearer, and the dot comes back.

What you have found is your blind spot, and you have had it all your life. At the back of the eye lies the retina, a thin layer of cells that respond to light: rods, which work best in dim light, and cones, which detect color and fine detail. These cells pass their signals to nerve fibers, and the fibers, roughly a million of them, gather into a single bundle, the optic nerve, which leaves the eye on its way to the brain. Where that bundle exits, there is room for no light-sensitive cells at all. Light that falls on that small patch, called the optic disc, is simply lost.

The French scientist Edme Mariotte described the spot in the 1660s. What is more puzzling than the hole is how seldom anyone notices it. The blind spot is far from tiny: it covers a patch of the visual field many times wider than the full moon appears in the sky. Part of the explanation is that we usually see with two eyes, and the two blind spots fall on different parts of the scene, so each eye covers for the other. Our eyes also move constantly, several times a second, so any one part of the world spends only a moment in the gap.

Yet even with one eye closed and the gaze held still, people do not see a black hole. They see whatever surrounds it. Draw the dot on lined paper and it disappears, but the lines seem to run straight through the place where it was. The brain, getting silence from that patch, fills it with a guess based on its edges: the same color, the same pattern, the line continuing on its way. Researchers call this "filling in," and it is one small example of a larger fact about vision: what we experience as seeing is partly built by the brain from incomplete information.

Some eyes lack the problem entirely. In humans and other vertebrates, the nerve fibers run across the front of the retina, between the incoming light and the light-sensitive cells, so they must pass back through the retina to leave the eye. The eye of an octopus developed separately and is arranged the other way around, with the fibers behind the cells, and it has no blind spot. Ours makes up for its arrangement with a second eye, a restless gaze, and a brain that paints over the gap so smoothly that most people go their whole lives without suspecting it is there.

original_item.passage:
Draw a small cross on a card, and about three inches to its right a dot the size of a pencil eraser. Close your left eye, stare at the cross with your right, and slowly bring the card toward your face. At a distance of roughly a foot, the dot will vanish. Keep looking at the cross and move the card a little nearer, and the dot comes back.

What you have found is your blind spot, and you have had it all your life. At the back of the eye lies the retina, a thin layer of cells that respond to light: rods, which work best in dim light, and cones, which detect color and fine detail. These cells pass their signals to nerve fibers, and the fibers, roughly a million of them, gather into a single bundle, the optic nerve, which leaves the eye on its way to the brain. Where that bundle exits, there is room for no light-sensitive cells at all. Light that falls on that small patch, called the optic disc, is simply lost.

The French scientist Edme Mariotte described the spot in the 1660s. What is more puzzling than the hole is how seldom anyone notices it. The blind spot is far from tiny: it covers a patch of the visual field many times wider than the full moon appears in the sky. Part of the explanation is that we usually see with two eyes, and the two blind spots fall on different parts of the scene, so each eye covers for the other. Our eyes also move constantly, several times a second, so any one part of the world spends only a moment in the gap.

Yet even with one eye closed and the gaze held still, people do not see a black hole. They see whatever surrounds it. Draw the dot on lined paper and it disappears, but the lines seem to run straight through the place where it was. The brain, getting silence from that patch, fills it with a guess based on its edges: the same color, the same pattern, the line continuing on its way. Researchers call this "filling in," and it is one small example of a larger fact about vision: what we experience as seeing is partly built by the brain from incomplete information.

Some eyes lack the problem entirely. In humans and other vertebrates, the nerve fibers run across the front of the retina, between the incoming light and the light-sensitive cells, so they must pass back through the retina to leave the eye. The eye of an octopus developed separately and is arranged the other way around, with the fibers behind the cells, and it has no blind spot. Ours makes up for its arrangement with a second eye, a restless gaze, and a brain that paints over the gap so smoothly that most people go their whole lives without suspecting it is there.
